extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, natural history, and classification
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for constructing natural classifications (orders, families, genera) and a systematic taxonomy of logical fallacies — how to detect, classify, and avoid them. Useful for evaluating classification schemes and reasoning processes in scientific, legal, and practical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main principle of division: natural affinity / natural groups
rubrics_metrics.description: "The main principle of division must of course be natural affinity; the classes formed must be natural groups; and the formation of these has already been sufficiently treated of."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups should be formed according to natural affinities (the most important characters). Groups must not put together things that belong at different points of the general scale; classification should reflect real, natural groupings rather than arbitrary distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary divisions grounded on distinctions tied to the main phenomenon's degree
rubrics_metrics.description: "The primary divisions must be grounded not on all distinctions indiscriminately, but on those which correspond to variations in the degree of the main phenomenon."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing primary divisions, favor distinctions that mark variations in the intensity/degree of the principal phenomenon (e.g., Sensation, Thought, Voluntary Motion). Avoid using minor or unrelated differences as bases for primary splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break the series where variation in main phenomenon coincides with conspicuous property changes
rubrics_metrics.description: "The series of Animated Nature should be broken into parts at the points where the variation in the degree of the main phenomenon... begins to be attended by conspicuous changes in the miscellaneous properties of the animal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examples: boundaries at which Mammalia ends, Fishes are separated from Insects, Insects from Mollusca. Use conspicuous changes in many properties as signals to cut the series into primary groups so that each group corresponds to a definite portion of the scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of families/genera should reflect upward/downward gradient in scale
rubrics_metrics.description: "In like manner each family should, if possible, be so subdivided, that one portion of it shall stand higher and the other lower, though of course contiguous, in the general scale; and only when this is impossible is it allowable to ground the remaining subdivisions on characters having no determinable connection with the main phenomenon."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within families aim to arrange subordinate groups so that they occupy contiguous positions in the overall scale (one higher, one lower). Resort to characters unrelated to the main phenomenon only when no determinable gradient can be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where principal phenomenon dominates, prioritize the most important characters
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where the principal phenomenon so far transcends in importance all other properties on which a classification could be grounded... the first principle of a natural arrangement, that of forming the groups according to the most important characters."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one phenomenon overwhelmingly determines the nature of the subjects (e.g., animated existence), deviations from the gradient rule are guarded against by prioritizing the most significant characters when forming groups. Historical example/critique: Cuvier over-weighted mode of alimentation; Blainville better represented the scale by principal groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of natural arrangement apply beyond biology (art, business, law)
rubrics_metrics.description: "These principles are applicable to all cases in which mankind are called upon to bring the various parts of any extensive subject into mental co-ordination... The proper arrangement, for example, of a code of laws, depends on the same scientific conditions as the classifications in natural history."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same scientific conditions of natural arrangement when organizing extensive subjects in art, business, law, or other domains. Study of natural classification is recommended as preparatory discipline for codification and other organizational tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue apparent evidences that are not real evidence (definition of fallacies)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A catalogue of the varieties of apparent evidence which are not real evidence, is an enumeration of Fallacies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing arguments, enumerate and recognize types of apparent evidence that can mislead. The purpose is to identify what may be mistaken for evidence so that errors arising from moral or intellectual causes can be prevented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Fallacies of Inference vs Fallacies of Simple Inspection (a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first great distinction, that between Fallacies of Inference and Fallacies of Simple Inspection... This class, comprehending the whole of what may be termed Natural Prejudices, and which I shall call indiscriminately Fallacies of Simple Inspection or Fallacies a priori, shall be placed at the head of our list."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify erroneous beliefs into those arising from improper inference (drawing wrong conclusions from evidence) and those embraced without extrinsic evidence (self-evident or presumption-based). 'A priori' fallacies include natural prejudices and cases where inspection alone creates insufficient presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion: vagueness, ambiguity, or shifting premises
rubrics_metrics.description: "This gives existence to a class of fallacies which may be justly termed... Fallacies of Confusion; comprehending, among others, all those which have their source in language, whether arising from the vagueness or ambiguity of our terms, or from casual associations with them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for cases where premises are not conceived with due clearness or where different conceptions are used at different stages (collecting evidence vs using it). Many fallacies arise from suppressed, vague, or ambiguous steps; clarifying terms and making implicit premises explicit helps diagnose these errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify fallacies as inductive or deductive and by whether premises are false or inconclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Apparent Evidence may be either particular facts, or foregone generalizations... This gives us first, Fallacies of Induction and Fallacies of Deduction, and then a subdivision of each of these, according as the supposed evidence is false, or true but inconclusive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a bad argument, determine whether it simulates induction (generalizing from facts) or deduction (ratiocination from general propositions), and further whether the apparent evidence is itself false or true but insufficient to support the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Observation: errors from erroneous or insufficient facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "Fallacies of Induction, where the facts on which the induction proceeds are erroneous, may be termed Fallacies of Observation... whether the cause of failure be malobservation, or simple non-observation..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the factual basis of inductive claims. Errors due to bad observation include malobservation, non-observation, or reliance on intermediate marks that do not prove what they are supposed to prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization: correct facts but unwarranted general conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The other class of inductive fallacies, in which the facts are correct, but the conclusion not warranted by them, are properly denominated Fallacies of Generalization..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extending conclusions beyond what the evidence supports. Assess sample size, representativeness, and alternative explanations before generalizing from observed cases to broader laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Ratiocination: premises (though stated) do not support the conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: "There remain... those in which the premises of the ratiocination do not bear out its conclusion; the various cases, in short, of vicious argumentation, provided against by the rules of the syllogism. We shall call these, Fallacies of Ratiocination."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check deductive validity: even true premises can fail to entail the conclusion. Identify unsound syllogistic forms and invalid inferential steps that render a purported deduction fallacious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect suppressed premises and supply/test them
rubrics_metrics.description: "In all arguments... some of the links are suppressed... In order to detect the fallacy, the proposition thus silently assumed must be supplied... his confuter... must himself judge what the suppressed premise ought to be in order to support the conclusion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an argument seems to reach a dubious conclusion, reconstruct the implicit premises that would be required to make it valid; then evaluate those premises for truth and relevance. Example: ambiguous assumption about 'every distressed country is under a tyranny' vs converse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for moral (bias/indifference) vs intellectual causes of error
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sources of erroneous opinions are twofold, moral and intellectual... the moral do not fall within the compass of this work... They may be classed under two general heads: Indifference to the attainment of truth, and Bias... the moral causes of opinions... do not act directly, but by means of the intellectual causes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that bias and indifference act indirectly by distorting evidence-gathering and attention. Guard against biased attention and unequal weighting of evidence; strengthening intellectual methods (rigorous induction, attention to inconclusive evidence) mitigates moral causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify fallacies by cause of apparent evidentiary status or by type of evidence simulated
rubrics_metrics.description: "We may arrange them, at our choice, on either of two principles; according to the cause which makes them appear to be evidence, not being so; or according to the particular kind of evidence which they simulate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two complementary taxonomies are valuable: (a) group fallacies by why they look evidentiary (e.g., association, presumption, misleading marks), and (b) group them by what sort of correct reasoning they imitate (induction, deduction, observation). Use both to analyze errors comprehensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of a priori assumptions: confusing subjective ideas with objective realities
rubrics_metrics.description: "Illicit assumptions a priori consist in... mistaking subjective facts for objective, laws of the percipient mind for laws of the perceived object, properties of the ideas or conceptions for properties of the things conceived."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept intuitive or 'self-evident' propositions without testing. Distinguish between ideas in the mind and facts about external objects; avoid projecting the structure of thought onto the world without empirical or logical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware associative thinking: co-occurrence in thought does not imply co-occurrence in fact
rubrics_metrics.description: "A large proportion of the erroneous thinking... proceeds on a tacit assumption, that the same order must obtain among the objects in nature which obtains among our ideas of them. That if we always think of two things together, the two things must always exist together."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and challenge inferences based solely on habitual mental associations. Correlation in thought or experience does not guarantee causal or necessary connection in reality; require independent corroboration.
